extras.title: Herodian Judea
extras.note: A Roman client kingdom; dates combine Herod’s kingdom and Archelaus’s reduced ethnarchy.

extras.title: Anatolian beyliks
extras.note: Many rival principalities emerged in a landscape of weakening Seljuq, Mongol, and Byzantine control.

extras.title: British occupation & mandate project in Iraq
extras.note: Wartime occupation, a mandate project, and treaty supervision overlapped with the monarchy established in 1921.

extras.title: French mandate: Syria & Lebanon
extras.wikiTitle: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon
extras.note: French rule created and reorganized several administrations, not one enduring national state.

extras.title: Lebanon · independent state
extras.note: Independence in 1943 and final French troop withdrawal in 1946 were separate milestones.

extras.title: Syria · independent state
extras.note: Independence involved wartime recognition and transfer of power followed by French withdrawal in 1946.

extras.title: Kingdom of Hejaz & Nejd
extras.note: Ibn Saud’s dominions followed conquest and consolidation of distinct regions; this was not all Arabia.

extras.title: British Mandate for Palestine
extras.location: Eastern Mediterranean · west of the Jordan River
extras.note: British administration followed Ottoman defeat; Transjordan was administered separately.

extras.title: Emirate of Transjordan
extras.note: An autonomous Arab administration within the mandate framework; its provisions differed from Palestine west of the Jordan.

extras.title: Jordan · independent kingdom
extras.note: Independent as Transjordan in 1946, later renamed Jordan; borders and territorial claims changed.

extras.title: Palestine Liberation Organization
extras.note: A national representative organization, not a country or an unchanged government.

extras.title: Deccan sultanates
extras.note: Five major sultanates succeeded Bahmanid fragmentation; their political relations changed repeatedly.

extras.title: Durrani Empire
extras.note: Durrani rule had regional continuations and a British-backed restoration after this principal phase.

extras.title: Afghanistan · Barakzai rule
extras.note: Emirs and kings ruled with interruptions; territory and foreign-policy independence changed.

extras.title: Afghanistan · later regimes
extras.note: Groups republican, communist, wartime, and Taliban governments; these are distinct regimes, including Taliban takeover in 2021.

connections.label: Urban culture
connections.summary: Uruk was a major center within the wider Sumerian urban landscape.
connections.note: This is cultural overlap, not one state succeeding another.

connections.label: Later city-state period
connections.summary: The Uruk urban phase preceded the Early Dynastic landscape of competing cities.
connections.note: Archaeological periods overlap locally; Uruk itself continued to exist.

connections.label: Sargon’s conquests
connections.summary: Sargon brought numerous Mesopotamian city-states under Akkadian imperial rule.
connections.note: Conquest did not erase Sumerian cities or language.

connections.label: Scribal inheritance
connections.summary: Old Babylonian scribes copied and transmitted Sumerian literature.
connections.note: A cultural relationship spanning intervening dynasties, not immediate political succession.

connections.label: Sack of Babylon
connections.summary: A Hittite raid ended Babylon’s first dynasty.
connections.note: The attackers withdrew; this was not permanent Hittite rule of Babylonia.

connections.label: Kassite consolidation
connections.summary: Kassite rulers gradually consolidated Babylonia after the first dynasty’s collapse.
connections.note: The transition is obscure and included rival southern rulers.

connections.label: Assyrian occupation
connections.summary: Tukulti-Ninurta I conquered Babylon during Kassite rule.
connections.note: The Kassite dynasty survived this intervention.

connections.label: Elamite campaigns
connections.summary: Elamite attacks brought the Kassite dynasty to an end.
connections.note: Subsequent Babylonian dynasties, not lasting Elamite annexation, followed.

connections.label: Renewed expansion
connections.summary: Later Assyrian kings renewed expansion after a period of contraction.
connections.note: Middle and Neo-Assyrian are modern period labels, not a single dated founding event.

connections.label: Fall of Nineveh
connections.summary: Babylonian and Median forces destroyed the Assyrian capital of Nineveh.
connections.note: Assyrian resistance continued after 612; neither the people nor their culture vanished.

connections.label: Iranian languages
connections.summary: The Medes were among the Iranian-speaking groups recorded in western Iran.
connections.note: A linguistic category is not a unified ancestral empire.

connections.label: Cyrus defeats Astyages
connections.summary: Cyrus overthrew the Median ruler and incorporated Media into his growing empire.
connections.note: The extent and organization of an earlier Median empire remain debated.

connections.label: Capture of Babylon
connections.summary: Cyrus captured Babylon and incorporated Babylonia into Achaemenid rule.
connections.note: Local institutions and traditions continued under new imperial government.

connections.label: Susa & administration
connections.summary: Susa and Elamite administrative traditions became important within Achaemenid government.
connections.note: Elam’s diverse earlier kingdoms are not one dynasty directly replaced on a single date.

connections.label: Regional successor states
connections.summary: Independent southeastern states preserved some Hittite dynastic and cultural traditions after the empire fell.
connections.note: These included Luwian and Aramaean polities, not a single restored Hittite empire.

connections.label: Assyrian expansion
connections.summary: Assyrian expansion progressively absorbed Syro-Hittite kingdoms.
connections.note: Different kingdoms were conquered at different times.

connections.label: Fall of Croesus
connections.summary: Cyrus defeated Lydia and brought western Anatolia under Persian rule.
connections.note: The conventional dating varies slightly across chronologies.

connections.label: Artistic exchange
connections.summary: Samaria’s ivories show exchanges with Phoenician and Syrian neighbors.
connections.note: Shared artistic forms do not prove a shared political identity.

connections.label: Capture of Samaria
connections.summary: Assyrian conquest ended the northern kingdom and deported part of its population.
connections.note: People remained in the region; this was not the disappearance of all Israelites.

connections.label: Jerusalem destroyed
connections.summary: Babylonian forces destroyed Jerusalem’s temple and deported part of Judah’s population.
connections.note: The exiles were not all inhabitants, and Jewish history continued in several places.

connections.label: Persian imperial rule
connections.summary: Phoenician cities came under Achaemenid rule while maintaining important maritime roles.
connections.note: Their earlier city-state independence was already constrained by several empires.

connections.label: Hasmonean autonomy
connections.summary: Hasmonean rulers gained autonomy amid Seleucid conflict and declining control of Judea.
connections.note: The revolt and independence were processes involving competing local factions.

connections.label: Roman-backed Herod
connections.summary: Herod captured Jerusalem with Roman support and displaced the last Hasmonean ruler.
connections.note: Roman involvement in Judea had begun earlier; Herod ruled as a client king.

connections.label: Roman patronage
connections.summary: Roman political and military support enabled Herod’s kingship.
connections.note: This relationship concerns Roman patronage, not an equal alliance.

connections.label: Seljuqs take Baghdad
connections.summary: Seljuq rulers took Baghdad and exercised military power alongside the Abbasid caliphate.
connections.note: The caliphate continued; the Seljuqs did not become a replacement caliphate.

connections.label: Battle of Manzikert
connections.summary: Seljuq forces defeated the Byzantine army at Manzikert, accelerating changes across Anatolia.
connections.note: Byzantium survived; settlement and political transformation took decades.

connections.label: Anatolian branch
connections.summary: A Seljuq branch established the Sultanate of Rûm in Anatolia.
connections.note: Related dynastic branches overlapped rather than splitting in a single treaty.

connections.label: Köse Dağ & overlordship
connections.summary: Mongol victory at Köse Dağ reduced the Sultanate of Rûm to dependent status.
connections.note: The Ilkhanate was established later; the 1243 attackers were a Mongol imperial army.

connections.label: Regional principalities
connections.summary: Declining Seljuq authority accompanied the growth of rival Anatolian principalities.
connections.note: Not every beylik originated in the same way or at the same time.

connections.label: Ottoman expansion
connections.summary: The Ottoman principality grew among these rivals and progressively absorbed many of them.
connections.note: The Ottomans were one beylik among several, not the automatic successor to all Seljuq lands.

connections.label: Regional dynastic context
connections.summary: The Ilkhanate and later regional dynasties form parts of this broad Iran–Iraq period.
connections.note: This umbrella entry is not a separate successor state.

connections.label: Timur’s campaigns
connections.summary: Timur conquered much of Iran and Iraq amid competing regional dynasties.
connections.note: The umbrella period includes multiple polities and overlapping zones of rule.

connections.label: Pahlavi dynasty
connections.summary: The Pahlavi dynasty replaced Qajar rule in Iran.
connections.note: The endpoint groups Pahlavi and later republican eras; the dedicated Iran map distinguishes 1979.

connections.label: British wartime occupation
connections.summary: British conquest of Ottoman Mesopotamia was followed by a mandate project and treaty arrangements.
connections.note: Postwar borders and institutions were contested, including during the Iraqi revolt of 1920.

connections.label: Faisal’s monarchy
connections.summary: Faisal became king in 1921 while British supervision continued until formal independence in 1932.
connections.note: The monarchy overlapped with British control rather than beginning after it ended.

connections.label: Republican coup
connections.summary: Army officers overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and proclaimed a republican government.
connections.note: Later republican regimes are grouped by the timeline, not treated as one unchanged government.

connections.label: French mandate rule
connections.summary: After Ottoman defeat and contested postwar settlement, Syria and Lebanon came under French mandate rule.
connections.note: This schematic omits the short-lived Arab Kingdom of Syria and several mandate subdivisions.

connections.label: Independence & withdrawal
connections.summary: Syria and Lebanon achieved independence through separate processes, completed by French troop withdrawal.
connections.note: Lebanon commemorates 1943; Syria commemorates the 1946 evacuation.

connections.label: Territorial consolidation
connections.summary: Ibn Saud’s expansion included taking al-Ahsa from Ottoman forces before later consolidating his dominions.
connections.note: Not all Saudi territories had been directly administered by the Ottomans.

connections.label: Kingdom proclaimed
connections.summary: The consolidated dominions were proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
connections.note: The proclamation followed years of conquest and administration; it was not a union of all Arabian states.

connections.label: British administration
connections.summary: British military conquest was followed by League of Nations mandate administration in Palestine.
connections.note: The population’s political rights and future were contested; this was not a consensual union.

connections.label: Separate administrations
connections.summary: Transjordan developed under a separate Arab administration within the wider mandate framework.
connections.note: The map’s Palestine node denotes territory west of the Jordan, not a claim that the emirate was carved from an already independent state.

connections.label: Independent kingdom
connections.summary: British recognition of Transjordan’s independence ended the mandate relationship there.
connections.note: Recognition, treaty effect, and the kingdom’s proclamation had different dates within 1946.

connections.label: Israel proclaimed
connections.summary: Israel was proclaimed as British rule ended, amid war in the former mandate territory.
connections.note: The 1947 UN partition proposal did not produce two functioning states as envisaged.

connections.label: Displacement & organizing
connections.summary: War, Palestinian displacement, and continuing national mobilization preceded the PLO’s establishment.
connections.note: A contextual political history link, not a transfer of British governmental authority to the PLO.

connections.label: Palestine proclaimed
connections.summary: The Palestine National Council proclaimed the State of Palestine, acknowledged by the UN General Assembly.
connections.note: Declaration and diplomatic recognition did not establish full territorial sovereignty or end occupation.

connections.label: Mutual recognition & Oslo
connections.summary: Israel and the PLO exchanged recognition and signed interim self-government arrangements.
connections.note: The accords did not settle final borders or create a sovereign Palestinian state.

connections.label: Long-distance trade
connections.summary: Indus and Mesopotamian societies participated in long-distance exchange networks.
connections.note: Trade links do not establish political union or population identity.

connections.label: Overlapping transformations
connections.summary: Late Harappan communities overlapped with changing Indo-Gangetic cultural landscapes.
connections.note: This is not a conquest or simple Harappan-to-Vedic state succession; language and identity remain research questions.

connections.label: Later regional states
connections.summary: Later Vedic textual traditions developed alongside the emergence of regional states in northern South Asia.
connections.note: Culture, texts, and states have different chronologies; there was no single Vedic empire.

connections.label: Magadhan consolidation
connections.summary: The Magadhan political core of the mahājanapadas was incorporated into the Mauryan imperial project.
connections.note: Not every mahājanapada survived until, or was conquered by, the Mauryas in the same way.

connections.label: Treaty & frontier
connections.summary: Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus established a negotiated frontier after conflict.
connections.note: A selected interstate encounter, not the descent of one empire from the other.

connections.label: Regional dynasties
connections.summary: After Mauryan power ended, numerous regional dynasties governed different parts of South Asia.
connections.note: The endpoint is a modern grouping, not one successor kingdom.

connections.label: Northwestern imperial setting
connections.summary: Kushan power formed one important part of the diverse post-Mauryan political landscape.
connections.note: An umbrella-to-member context link, not a single dynasty changing its name.

connections.label: Changing northern powers
connections.summary: As Kushan power contracted, Gupta rulers consolidated parts of northern India.
connections.note: Regional successors and intervening rulers existed; there was no wholesale handover of all Kushan lands.

connections.label: Regional rule expands
connections.summary: Gupta power fragmented as invasions and regional autonomy reshaped northern India.
connections.note: The post-Gupta label groups different kingdoms rather than one political successor.

connections.label: Harsha’s northern realm
connections.summary: Harsha’s kingdom was one major polity within the wider post-Gupta landscape.
connections.note: It did not reunite all former Gupta territories or govern all South Asia.

connections.label: Diplomatic missions
connections.summary: Harsha exchanged diplomatic missions with Tang China.
connections.note: Diplomatic contact is not territorial continuity.

connections.label: Regional courts
connections.summary: Following Harsha’s death, northern power again rested with multiple regional courts.
connections.note: Many kingdoms already existed beyond his control; this umbrella spans the wider subcontinent.

connections.label: Southern imperial center
connections.summary: The Cholas rose within a competitive southern landscape of regional dynasties.
connections.note: They were not the sole successors to northern post-Gupta kingdoms.

connections.label: Maritime raids
connections.summary: Chola naval forces attacked Srivijayan ports and centers in Southeast Asia.
connections.note: A campaign did not create permanent Chola rule over the whole Srivijayan maritime world.

connections.label: Northern sultanate expands
connections.summary: Conquest and consolidation established Delhi sultanate rule across parts of northern India.
connections.note: Many regional kingdoms survived; this was not the end of all pre-existing South Asian states.

connections.label: Deccan political setting
connections.summary: Vijayanagara emerged amid Delhi’s southern campaigns and a changing Deccan political landscape.
connections.note: This is regional context, not a claim that Vijayanagara was simply a renamed Delhi province.

connections.label: Babur’s victory
connections.summary: Babur defeated the Lodi ruler at Panipat and established Mughal rule in northern India.
connections.note: Mughal consolidation was prolonged and interrupted by Sur rule.

connections.label: Battle of Talikota
connections.summary: A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara and devastated its capital.
connections.note: The Vijayanagara dynasty continued from other capitals after 1565.

connections.label: Mughal annexations
connections.summary: Mughal campaigns absorbed major Deccan sultanates, culminating in the late 1680s.
connections.note: Different sultanates ended at different dates; this is a grouped regional account.

connections.label: Durrani state emerges
connections.summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani established a realm after Nader Shah’s death.
connections.note: Afsharid fragmentation produced several regional powers.

connections.label: Dost Mohammad in Kabul
connections.summary: Dost Mohammad consolidated Barakzai rule in Kabul after Durrani fragmentation.
connections.note: Regional rivals and later Durrani restoration complicate a simple dynasty-to-dynasty chain.

connections.label: First Anglo-Afghan War
connections.summary: British forces deposed Dost Mohammad and restored a Durrani ruler, then withdrew.
connections.note: Dost Mohammad subsequently returned to power.

connections.label: Foreign-policy independence
connections.summary: The Treaty of Rawalpindi recognized Afghanistan’s full foreign-policy independence after war.
connections.note: Afghanistan had not been an annexed province of British India.

connections.label: Monarchy overthrown
connections.summary: Daoud overthrew the monarchy and proclaimed a republic.
connections.note: The endpoint groups subsequent governments; it is not one unchanged republican regime.
